images.alt:
Transplanting light-dependent reactions for mammalian eye photosynthesis
Kuoran Xing 1, Yan Yan 2, Ziyu Zhu 3, Yinglu Chen 4, Glebert Cañete Dadol 4, Xiangji Pan 2, Siye Tong 4, Narattam Sikdar 4, Jinping Wang 5, Banglin Li 4, Mengfei Yu 6, Kai Jin 2, Xianguang Ding 7, Xiao Sun 8, Juan Ye 9, David Tai Leong 10
Affiliations Expand
PMID: 42143020 DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2026.04.034
Abstract
Mammalian eyes are exposed to visible light but cannot perform photosynthesis. Here, we show that introducing a nanoscale, structurally and functionally preserved thylakoid system, LEAF (light-reaction enriched thylakoid NADPH-foundry), into corneal cells enables light-driven bona fide photosynthetic production of NADPH and ATP, similar to plant leaves, which alleviates oxidative stress and inflammation. LEAF acts in two domains. Intracellularly, it integrates with host cells to supply NADPH and ATP via intact photosynthetic electron transport, restoring redox balance. Extracellularly, photosynthesized NADPH enhances endogeneous antioxidant enzyme activity and reduces reactive oxygen species in the local environment. These results establish a strategy for using light as an energy input in mammalian metabolic systems and suggest a possible cross-kingdom, endosymbiosis-like interaction in which animal cells derive functional benefits from plant-derived photosynthetic neo-organelles.

Keywords: cornea; eye; inflammation; light-dependent reactions; nanomedicine; organelle; photosynthesis; reactive oxygen species; thylakoid.

I am mildly surprised that my very first naive attempt already worked this well on top of what I thought was already a fairly manually well-tuned project.
This is a first for me because I am very used to doing the iterative optimization of neural network training manually. You come up with ideas, you implement them, you check if they work (better validation loss), you come up with new ideas based on that, you read some papers for inspiration, etc etc. This is the bread and butter of what I do daily for 2 decades. Seeing the agent do this entire worktlow end-to-end and all by itself as it worked through approx.

and all by itselt as it worked through approx. 700 changes autonomously is wild. It really looked at the sequence of results of experiments and used that to plan the next ones. It's not novel, ground-breaking "research" (yet), but all the adjustments are "real", I didn't find them manually previously, and they stack up and actually improved nanochat. Among the bigger things e.g.:
- It noticed an oversight that my parameterless QKnorm didn't have a scaler multiplier attached, so my attention was too diffuse. The agent found multipliers to sharpen it, pointing to future work.
- It found that the Value Embeddings really like regularization and I wasn't applying any (oops).
- It found that my banded attention was too conservative (i forgot to tune it).
- It found that AdamW betas were all messed up.
- It tuned the weight decay schedule.
- It tuned the network initialization.
This is on top of all the tuning I've already done over a good amount of time. The exact commit is here, from this "round 1" of autoresearch. I am going to kick off "round 2" , and in parallel l
am looking at how multiple agents can collaborate to unlock parallelism. github.com/karpathy/nanoc...

AII LLM frontier labs will do this. It's the final boss battle. It's a lot more complex at scale of course - you don't just have a single train. py file to tune. But doing it is "just engineering" and it's going to work. You spin up a swarm of agents, you have them collaborate to tune smaller models, you promote the most promising ideas to increasingly larger scales, and humans (optionally) contribute on the edges.
And more generally, *any* metric you care about that is reasonably efficient to evaluate (or that has more efficient proxy metrics such as training a smaller network) can be autoresearched by an agent swarm. It's worth thinking about whether your problem falls into this bucket too.

1/3 A you choose a car, all branches are kept

external.title: A Slower Speed of Light – MIT Game Lab
external.description: A Slower Speed of Light is a first-person game prototype in which players navigate a 3D space while picking up orbs that reduce the speed of light in increments. Custom-built, open-source relativistic graphics code allows the speed of light in the game to approach the player’s own maximum walking speed. Visual effects of special relativity gradually become apparent to the player, increasing the challenge of gameplay. These effects, rendered in realtime to vertex accuracy, include the Doppler effect (red- and blue-shifting of visible light, and the shifting of infrared and ultraviolet light into the visible spectrum); the searchlight effect (increased brightness in the direction of travel); time dilation (differences in the perceived passage of time from the player and the outside world); Lorentz transformation (warping of space at near-light speeds); and the runtime effect (the ability to see objects as they were in the past, due to the travel time of light). Players can choose to share their mastery and experience of the game through Twitter. A Slower Speed of Light combines accessible gameplay and a fantasy setting with theoretical and computational physics research to deliver an engaging and pedagogically rich experience.

children.text: i don't think understanding what's going on is the bottleneck here. humans are already shockingly good at assessing this stuff, even if often subconsciously. the problem is that even if you know about the coalition, that doesn't make the coalition's value proposition less attractive to its members.

how do you plan, once you've determined that anti-AI people of the leftist Benderite mold are repeating propaganda talking points conforming to a certain hostile vision of AI because all their friends and respected authority figures are also doing it, to change that latter situation?

the thing that sustains these coalitions is not lack of knowledge, among the coalition members *or* among members of opposing coalitions (thats us on the pro-AI side, here). i do not think you can escape from these situations by manufacturing more knowledge or better distributing it.
That surprises me! I thought building agreement about objective reality was your thing!
I also disagree that lack of knowledge isn’t what holds coalitions together; you know how the trans cults of personality work, you know that information management is key to the BITE model.

ah, you're assuming causation has to run lack of knowledge->coalition, but i'm actually arguing (not well, in the length limits, sorry) that coalition->lack of knowledge. a lack of knowledge is there, it just isn't the cause or sustainment mechanism for the coalition's existence.

rather, the lack of knowledge is in large part a choice made so as to stay within the coalition. that's why most of them refuse to even try AI tools in the first place! knowledge of how AI tools actually perform would not be beneficial, and could even be detrimental, to their social position.

and yeah, i am the "building agreement about objective reality" gal but it turns out objective reality has some things to say about how coalitions of humans actually work rather than how i'd like them to work :)

which is one of the reasons i'm mad about social media lately lol.

you can align the social incentives of humans in the direction of objective reality somewhat, but its stuff like institutions and social norms. "academic science" is such a thing, imperfect as it is. we can hopefully build better ones. but that's a different project than individual outreach.

put another way, when i asked my TPOT friends about AI 18 months ago I knew I was doing something that would threaten my position in the social graph. I did it anyway, for various reasons, including that I didn't have just one social graph i was part of. I was picking one coalition out of several.

if you have reason to believe someone is on the fence, already respects people from multiple distinct social graphs/coalitions with different views on the topic in question, i could see them being an individual outreach candidate. but most people aren't like that.

Why does the outreach have to be individual?

I concede that my idea is not a panacea; the attack on coalitionism must be multi-pronged. This is one of the prongs.

If it saves only people at the fringes, that’s far better than saving no one, and it’s a first step toward saving more.
attack on coalitionism? do you imagine that you are outside a coalition yourself, or that you can be?

No lmao, it was a spur of the moment phrase, not a battle cry. “Coalitionism” should here be construed as referring to these types of inimical coalitions, not the broad sense of forming coalitions in general. 😅

fair enough. i don't actually disagree with the project of trying to convince people or build bridges, in a way i'm here doing that too. but i do think some people are probably bad candidates and i think that guy was one of those lol.
Infrastructure for the good candidates, personal tilting at windmills for the bad ones. 😁

TPOT in general is (was?) derided specifically for encouraging that sort of lack-of-commitment-to-one-coalition, an openness to social connections that in other social clusters would be verboten. most people on twitterlikes are *not* operating like that, at least not online.

i actually think one of the problems with social media is that encourages/forces near-total transparency. you can't be a slightly different person with different groups of people, experiment with different beliefs and roles with some privacy. you are always exposed to everyone.
This is also a problem, yes, and I agree that my proposal does not solve it, and in isolation or incautiously implemented it could even exacerbate it.

this seems to encourage hard commitment to one coalition and ostentatious signaling of membership in the chosen coalition, by harassing people your coalition doesn't like, or enduring and calling out the harassment of an enemy coalition, saying cruel things about them, etc.

Ok, here's my map of this whole argument including my assumption of how the participants would rate each claim.
fenc.es/Flo/infrasou...

If you want to convince me that infrasound is harmful, start here to figure out which is the actual crux between us: fenc.es/Flo/infrasou...

images.alt: Screenshot of a Fenc.es argument tree. Root claim "Infrasound Harms At DC Levels": "Inaudible infrasound at the exposure levels observed near residential data centers causes measurable harm to human health." Confidence: 1% (strongly disagree). Supporting argument "Residents show Symptoms" (+): "Residents near some data centers report a cluster of symptoms: headaches, fatigue, concentration problems, mood changes, nausea, dizziness, sleep disruption, anxiety, tinnitus, and palpitations, which they attribute to #infrasound." Confidence 85, weight 3.1. Opposing argument "Studies Find No Effect" (−): "Under blinded controlled exposure and in large epidemiological surveys, no physiological or psychological effect of ambient-level infrasound has been found. Where measurable effects have been found or implied the methodology was lacking." Confidence 85, weight −4.8. Opposing argument "Dose Gap Kills The Claim" (−): "Residential DC infrasound sits far below any exposure level at which harm has been experimentally demonstrated, on a logarithmic scale." Confidence 90, weight −15. Opposing argument "Infrasound from Other Sources is not Harmful" (−): "If sub-perception infrasound at residential levels caused harm, we would have detected it by now. Every major national health body that has reviewed the evidence has concluded no effect, and the natural and industrial environments we've lived in for decades to centuries produce infrasound at comparable or higher levels without producing the claimed symptom cluster. The absence of effect where we'd most expect to find it is evidence the effect isn't real." Confidence 90, weight −15.

Screenshot of a Fenc.es argument tree comparison view. Root claim "Infrasound Harms At DC Levels": "Inaudible infrasound at the exposure levels observed near residential data centers causes measurable harm to human health." Compared perspectives: Andy Masley, Flo, Bear Smith, Benn Jordan (all by Flo), σ 36pp. Root confidence: Andy Masley strongly disagree, Flo strongly disagree, Bear Smith disagree (faded), Benn Jordan strongly agree. Argument "Dose Gap Kills The Claim": "Residential DC infrasound sits far below any exposure level at which harm has been experimentally demonstrated, on a logarithmic scale." Confidences: Andy Masley 97, Flo 90, Bear Smith 55, Benn Jordan 90, σ 16. Argument "Studies Find No Effect": "Under blinded controlled exposure and in large epidemiological surveys, no physiological or psychological effect of ambient-level infrasound has been found. Where measurable effects have been found or implied the methodology was lacking." Confidences: Andy Masley 92, Flo 85, Bear Smith 65, Benn Jordan 25, σ 26. Argument "Residents show Symptoms": "Residents near some data centers report a cluster of symptoms: headaches, fatigue, concentration problems, mood changes, nausea, dizziness, sleep disruption, anxiety, tinnitus, and palpitations, which they attribute to #infrasound." This one is so much fun!!

I think you'll like it, it's very math

And unlike the other stuff that lord help me but I can't get into a thread, I can do this in like four bisks

So, I'm not gonna motivate this part, but a lot of folks have at various times thought (what I think is true) that the world is pure structure

That's a substantive thesis about the physical world, or consciousness or philosophy or whatever

But how to model it mathematically?

In fact, we have really good models of carrier free structure in like, homotopy type theory; or in category theory; or you can be lazy and say "whatever it is that isomorphism preserves for groups"

Awodey's principle of univalence rules here:

www.andrew.cmu.edu/user/awodey/...

But, historically, this is *not* the resource (analytic) philosophy has used

Instead, they've tried to model a structured world as relations on sets

(This is, 100 years on, still somehow popular? Unbelievable...)

It breaks for two big reasons

The first reason has been known since 1928, it's "Newman's reply to Russell"

Basically, sets are relationally promiscuous up to their cardinality

Since a relation is just a set of tuples of elements, if you have a set W, you have *every relation of that cardinality or less* in the subset W × W

In other words, if you think a carrier set of simples underlies a relation R, then that carrier set gives you every single other relation for free automatically, which is incredibly awkward if you want your theory to say anything substantive about anything

You need to privilege a relation

But we really should have known this already 

The point is to model the world structurally

And the building blocks of a set are "bare individuals" whose only property is their individuation, which is already a non-structural contribution

So even before Newman, we should have known set theory was a bad model of structure

It's like tossing a chicken in a stewpot & trying to find a way to stir to make it vegan

It isn't like the whole field makes this mistake

I might disagree with them for being metaphysical, but folks like Ladyman and Ross don't make this mistake in their 'Ontic Structural Realism' theory

But, even today, many analytic structuralists do use sets as their model

And back in the 20th century?

It was *bad* they literally all did it, almost like using set theory was some crazy culture war thing to distinguish them from, God forbid, continental phenomenologists

Anyway, a structuralist who wants to think about this stuff mathematically has many options but category theory or univalence are good & "meh isomorphism" is good enough if the dog ate your homework

But for the love of God do not provision objective reality with a set of simples or you're hosed

Honestly I think set theory's fine for this task

The other options can make certain things inarticulable in the theory which is a plus if you were aiming at that anyway, but nothing's ever stopping you from emulating it in set theory

There's a conservation of specificity here, it doesn't really /

matter whether you make your choices about what should be articulable in the metatheory or in the theory or in objects inside the theory because all of these divisions are made up and the points don't matter

It's like how second-order arithmetic is "canonical" but second-order logic itself can't be pinned down, so by making arithmetic canonical you just remove canonicity from logic and ultimately just moved the slack around rather than reduced it

Well it is fine as a model of course no one disputes that! I'm not saying, "don't model things with sets" that is perfectly well permitted

It's a question about what is objectively real

And if we want to be able to make substantive claims about what exists in the world, or at least if we want that to be possible in principle, we cannot say that the structure of the world is the structure of relations on sets of simples

If you say, "well the atoms in the sand on the beach are bare individuals and the laws of physics are relations that act on those simples" then you've *by logical neccessity* created a googleplex alien relations among those atoms, which we really should not want

I don't really see how you've "created" these relations in any way that's supposed to present a problem for this project

If we're modeling the world via relations we're busy distinguishing relations anyway, that's how we're getting off the ground, so having lots of extra relations is harmless
More specifically(?), I don't see why we'd try to identify the ∃ of our set theory with the existence enjoyed by physical reality
I kind of feel like I'm missing some motivation here

More generally it's not clear that this sort of thing could be done even in principle

What I have in mind is, maybe every structure that contains the physical world as a substructure is only possible to generate (qua theory) via relations and operators that cannot all enjoy full-blooded existence

There's a huge literature about this stuff (search term: Newman problem) but the basic impetus is that we want two things:

- We want to say something about the real structure of the universe (at least in principle)

- We don't want to commit in advance to picking out a "privileged relation"

When you say, "ignore the mathematical existential ∃, just identify physical reality in another way", you're asking to privilege a relation by distinguishing one of them in another way

saying, not that ∃ some relation, but that, that relation is "really real"
That is a solution, and you're allowed to think that that's right; that there is some relation between individuals in the physical world that is "really real"

But there's philopsophy reasons to debate it, it is a debate:

one reason to be skeptical is that which relation is priveledged beyond the existential quantifier is an intrinsically non-structural fact, and it's hard to say how we'd be acquainted with it

I'd need a more careful presentation of this to see the sense in which it's a puzzle, otherwise I suspect we're just dropping modals here

I guess my general shrug is that "the ∃ of [this theory]" and "the [P] of [this theory]" each have the same total arbitrariness in the brackets, so why care

I mean it's true that you can get the same content in the different models if you do careful bookkeeping about what relations are merely existentially quantified & which ones are really real; if you think you know some structure you think you know it & you can model it variously

But the set at that point isn't really doing any work, it's just a carrier for you to use to display the relation

And that's fine, but it's just a lot more moving parts that goes to the same thing

"What's really real is some shape we can describe using this special priveleged relation on this set"
The crucial thing is that you don't add the set into the inventory of objectivity

If you use the set W as a model to conveniently display the shape of a relation I think the most that can be said against it is that it's not very economical & you have to keep two books (what is "real" vs what is "just the model")

The why care is basically just, if we present the structure of the world in a messy way and keep two books we could get confused

And if God forbid we get a thought like "what is really real isn't the shape R displayed by this choice of set and relation as a model" then we're instantly hosed

With carrier free structure we don't need to keep two books, we just add what we think is real to the inventory of objective reality

And we don't need to incorporate 'non structural' things (a set of bare elements) into a presentation of a structure

But yes if you're willing to keep ∃ as purely a mathematical quantifier in the model and say "it has got nothing really to do with what is real" you can do what you describe and it is okay if (imo) cumbersome

Moreover you can cut the problem off at the root by just not putting a set into the inventory of objective reality

The reason for putting the set was to describe some relations, some structure, and we might have thought we needed a carrier set to do that

But you don't need it! Math foundations gives us a better object, carrier-free structure, which captures the intuition that what we care about in the structure of a group is what isomorphism preserves, not that there underlying simples distinguished by bare individuation
